Current policy · SNAP and Medicaid

Work Rules, Lost Benefits

What the work rules in the 2025 federal budget law, H.R. 1, take from SNAP and Medicaid in Hawaiʻi in a full year: how many people lose benefits, how much federal money leaves the state, and what the law moves onto the State’s budget.

Hawaiʻi Appleseed · Model run November 22, 2026 · A full year under the new rules, 2027

39,140
Adults lose Medicaid, of 129,577 in the expansion group; 24,400 to 51,800 across the assumptions below.
7,250
Adults lose SNAP under the wider time limit; 4,950 to 9,630 across the assumptions.
$204 million
Federal money lost a year: $171 million for Medicaid and $33 million in SNAP benefits.
$106 million
SNAP costs moved to the State each year from October 2027, for benefits and administration.

What the Law Changes

THE 2025 FEDERAL BUDGET LAW cut SNAP and Medicaid largely through paperwork. It widens who must prove they work to keep food assistance, adds a monthly work test to Medicaid for adults covered under the Affordable Care Act’s expansion, renews that coverage twice as often, and shifts part of SNAP’s cost from the federal government to the states.1

SNAP’s three-month time limit, which ends benefits for adults who do not work or train 80 hours a month, now reaches adults 55 to 64, parents whose youngest child is 14 or older, and veterans, houseless residents and former foster youth, whom it used to exempt. The Department of Human Services applied the new rules on November 1, 2025.2

For Medicaid, adults 19 to 64 in the expansion group must show 80 hours of work, service or school, or $580 of income, in one of the six months before each renewal. Med-QUEST3 begins on January 1, 2027, and will not remove anyone for it before July.4 The estimates here describe a full year once the rules are in force.

Who the SNAP Rules Reach

ABOUT 20,920 ADULTS on SNAP fall under the three-month time limit for the first time, most of them between 55 and 64. Of those, 7,840 are exempt because of a disability or another recognized reason, and 3,160 already work at least 20 hours a week. The other 9,910 have to find work or a training slot, or prove an exemption, within three months.5

These counts come from the federal government’s audit sample of active SNAP cases, which records each household member’s age, disability, work registration and hours the way a caseworker sees them. The Department estimated about 16,000 members aged 55 to 64 newly covered; the audit sample gives 16,420.6

How many of those adults actually lose SNAP is the estimate’s main assumption. In Virginia, the time limit cut participation among the adults it covered by 53 percent, with no gain in employment.7 A national study found more than a third leaving.8 The middle case here assumes 70 percent of adults who neither work nor qualify for an exemption lose SNAP, and a few who should keep it lose it anyway. The low and high cases use 50 and 90 percent.

The figures leave out adults 18 to 54 without children, who were already under the time limit when Hawaiʻi’s statewide waiver ended on June 30, 2024; the audit sample shows 6,910 of them neither working 20 hours nor exempt. Maui and Kauaʻi counties kept a waiver until June 30, 2025,9 and the new law’s test for a waiver rules out another, so these estimates are low by whatever a renewed waiver would have protected there.

Deeper Poverty for People Already Below the Line

MOST ADULTS WHO LOSE SNAP have almost nothing else. In the middle case, 52 percent of them live in SNAP households with countable income under half the federal poverty line, and 32 percent have no countable income at all. The average adult who loses SNAP loses $407 a month, about 27 percent of their household’s income and benefits together.

The Census Bureau’s Supplemental Poverty Measure counts everyone a family shares resources with, and many adults who lose SNAP live with relatives whose earnings keep the family above the line. On that measure, 48 percent of the adults who lose SNAP are already in poverty before the cut. The cut pushes about 610 more people below the line, 50 of them children, and deepens poverty for those already there: the total shortfall below the line grows by $17.6 million, about 53 percent of the benefits lost.

Medicaid Coverage at Stake

MED-QUEST COVERED 129,577 ADULTS in the expansion group in September 2026.3 By the American Community Survey’s account of their work, school and family, 48 percent already meet the new test, 28 percent are exempt as parents of a child 13 or younger, people with a disability or for another reason the survey records, and 24 percent, about 30,780 adults, are neither.

In Arkansas, the only state to end coverage under a similar rule, more than 95 percent of the adults it covered already worked enough or should have been exempt, yet coverage among them fell by 13 percentage points, mostly because people could not get the reporting done.10 The middle case here assumes 80 percent of adults who neither work nor qualify for an exemption lose coverage, along with 9 percent of those who do, and that renewing coverage every six months drops another 5 percent of those still enrolled.11

Source: Hawaiʻi Appleseed estimates from the American Community Survey 2020–24, scaled to Med-QUEST enrollment. Federal dollars at $4,853 per expansion adult a year, 90 percent federal.12 The survey’s sampling range on the middle case is 37,920 to 40,360; the 2024 one-year survey gives 39,270.

The Department’s own estimate is 19,000 to 38,000 adults losing coverage from the two changes together.2 The middle case sits just above that range, likely because the survey cannot see many of the conditions that make someone medically frail and so exempt. Those adults would still have to prove it.

What the State Is Asked to Pay

FROM OCTOBER 2027, Hawaiʻi pays a share of SNAP benefits set by its payment error rate. The rate was 10.92 percent in federal fiscal year 2025,13 which puts Hawaiʻi in the top tier: 15 percent of benefits, about $91.1 million a year at current issuance.14 The State may use its 2026 rate instead, not yet published, and each tier lower cuts the bill by about $30.4 million. The State also now pays three-quarters of SNAP’s administrative costs, about $14.8 million more a year.2

Benefits, error rate 6 to 8 percent: 5 percent share30.4
Benefits, error rate 8 to 10 percent: 10 percent share60.7
Benefits, error rate 10 percent or more: 15 percent share91.1
Benefits on Hawaiʻi’s fiscal year 2025 rate, 10.92 percent: 15 percent share91.1

Source: Public Law 119-21, sections 10105 and 10106; Hawaiʻi Appleseed estimates on $607 million of benefits a year, the Department’s issuance from July to September 2026 at an annual rate.

Medicaid works the other way. Each adult who loses coverage saves the State its 10 percent share, about $19.0 million a year in the middle case, while $171.0 million in federal money leaves Hawaiʻi’s clinics and hospitals. Covering those adults with state funds would cost about $190.0 million a year.

County and District Figures

EVERY COUNTY LOSES COVERAGE AND FOOD AID, and Hawaiʻi County loses the most Medicaid coverage for its size, about 4.1 percent of its residents. The American Community Survey identifies nothing smaller than areas of about 100,000 people, so these figures give each part of such an area that area’s average, weighted by where people lived in the 2020 census.15 The House and Senate districts are the 2022 plan, still in force. District figures carry the whole survey’s uncertainty and more: a district inside a large survey area cannot differ from it here.

What Comes Next

How many people lose benefits depends on choices still open to the State: how much Med-QUEST can confirm from records it already holds instead of asking enrollees, how quickly the Department can screen SNAP households for exemptions, and whether the Legislature funds the SNAP share when the first bill arrives in October 2027. Every adult kept on through better verification is food and care that stays in Hawaiʻi.

These figures will be updated as data from the first months under the new rules come in.

How These Estimates Are Calculated

THREE SOURCES, each used where it is strongest. SNAP’s work rules are applied to the federal audit sample of Hawaiʻi’s active SNAP cases, 571 households representing about 83,000, because only it records SNAP households as the program defines them. Medicaid is estimated from the American Community Survey’s adults who report Medicaid, scaled up to Med-QUEST’s enrollment, since the survey misses about a third of enrollees. Poverty and geography come from the survey population used on this site’s other pages.16

For the poverty estimate, SNAP is placed on survey households: every household that reports receiving it, plus eligible households drawn at random until the count matches the Department’s 77,980 households, with benefits under the October 2026 rules scaled to the Department’s issuance. Adults in those households are sorted into the same groups as in the audit sample, and each one’s chance of losing SNAP is set so that the survey reproduces the audit sample’s results group by group and dollar for dollar. Who loses SNAP is then drawn 2,000 times, and the poverty counts are the average.

The counts of who is subject, exempt and working are measured. The share of each group that loses benefits is assumed, because no data yet show how Hawaiʻi’s rules will play out. The ranges come from the research above: Virginia’s time limit for SNAP,7 and for Medicaid, Arkansas’s work requirement10 and the Congressional Budget Office’s national estimate.11

Table 10. The Assumptions Behind the Three Cases

Assumed share losing benefits (percent)LowMiddleHigh
SNAP: neither works nor exempt507090
SNAP: already meets the test0510
SNAP: exempt025
Medicaid: neither works nor exempt608095
Medicaid: meets the test or exempt2915
Medicaid: six-month renewals, of those still enrolled358

Not included: the SNAP changes to utility and internet deductions, the cap on future food-plan updates, Medicaid’s new limits on provider taxes and state-directed payments, cost sharing from October 2028, shorter retroactive coverage, the new limits on coverage for some lawfully present immigrants, and the end of enhanced marketplace premium credits. The estimates hold today’s population and wages fixed and allow for no change in work in response to the rules, which research on these programs has not found.7

Download the data

  • snap_losses.csv: adults losing SNAP and benefits lost by group and case, with sampling ranges (Table 3)
  • snap_adults.csv: SNAP adults by group and status (Table 2)
  • snap_income_depth.csv: income of the households that lose SNAP
  • poverty.csv: Supplemental Poverty Measure results by case (Table 4)
  • medicaid_losses.csv: Medicaid coverage and dollars lost by case, both survey files (Table 5)
  • medicaid_adults.csv: expansion adults by status
  • medicaid_groups.csv: survey counts against Med-QUEST enrollment
  • snap_state_cost.csv: SNAP costs moved to the State (Table 6)
  • by_geography.csv: every county and district, all three cases, with sampling errors (Tables 7 to 9)
  • snap_baseline_check.csv: SNAP on the survey population against the Department’s counts
  • snap_calibration.csv: the survey matched to the audit sample, group by group
  • summary.json: parameters and assumptions
  • manifest.json: run parameters, inputs and code version
